Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $H:D\to(0,\infty)$ be of class $C^3$, meaning that every partial derivative of total order at most three exists and is continuous. Set $\mathcal M:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times D$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, with global coordinates $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$; each coordinate is assigned length units, with $x^0=ct$ when a time coordinate is wanted. The function $H$ depends only on $(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ and is dimensionless.

Give $\mathcal M$ the coordinate orientation determined by $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$. Put $N_H:=H\partial_0$ and choose the time orientation whose future cone contains $N_H$; the lemma below proves that $N_H$ is timelike for the tensor defined here.

Define the symmetric coordinate tensor $g_H$ by
$$g_H=-H^{-2}(dx^0)^2+H^2\sum_{i=1}^3(dx^i)^2,$$
where $H^{-1}:=1/H$ and $H^{-2}:=(1/H)^2$. This exact coordinate form is called the positive-scalar conformastatic chart tensor in this item; no field equation or physical solution property is part of the definition.

Because $H>0$, the functions $H^{-1}$ and $H^{-2}$ are compositions and products of $H$ with positive-base powers of exponents $-1$ and $-2$. The derivative formula for these powers, repeated through any finite order, and closure of $C^k$ functions under composition and finite products show that the displayed coefficients are $C^3$ when $H$ is $C^3$, and smooth when $H$ is smooth.

For later component formulas define $H_i:=\partial_iH$, $H_{ij}:=\partial_i\partial_jH$, $q:=\sum_{i=1}^3H_i^2$, and $\Delta H:=\sum_{i=1}^3H_{ii}$.

derivations.claim: The coordinate matrix is diagonal and symmetric. Since $H>0$, all entries are nonzero, its inverse is $\operatorname{diag}(-H^2,H^{-2},H^{-2},H^{-2})$, and multiplying the two diagonal matrices gives the identity. The determinant is $(-H^{-2})(H^2)^3=-H^4<0$, so the matrix has exactly one negative and three positive diagonal entries and no zero eigenvalue. Thus it is nondegenerate of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ at every point. Its coefficients and inverse are C3 because $H$ is C3 and the reciprocal map $u\mapsto1/u$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$.

With the frame fields defined in the Statement, direct contraction against the diagonal matrix gives $g(n,n)=H^2(-H^{-2})=-1$, $g(n,e_i)=0$, and $g(e_i,e_j)=H^{-2}H^2\delta_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$. Each frame vector is a nonzero multiple of a distinct coordinate vector, so the four vectors form a basis. Their coordinate change matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(H,H^{-1},H^{-1},H^{-1})$, with positive determinant $H^{-2}$; hence the frame is positively oriented. The time orientation is the one specified in [F1], so $n$ is future-directed. The already computed metric determinant gives $\sqrt{|\det g|}=H^2$.

The formula is symmetric in $\beta,\gamma$, so the connection is torsion-free. Lowering its upper index gives $g_{\rho\alpha}\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\beta\gamma}=\tfrac12(\partial_\beta g_{\rho\gamma}+\partial_\gamma g_{\rho\beta}-\partial_\rho g_{\beta\gamma})$; adding the expressions with $(\rho,\gamma)$ interchanged cancels opposite derivative terms and yields $\partial_\beta g_{\rho\gamma}$, which is metric compatibility. Applying the formula to $g_{00}=-H^{-2}$ and $g_{ij}=H^2\delta_{ij}$ gives $\Gamma^0{}_{0i}=\tfrac12(-H^2)(2H^{-3}H_i)=-H_i/H$, $\Gamma^i{}_{00}=-\tfrac12H^{-2}(2H^{-3}H_i)=-H_i/H^5$, and $\Gamma^i{}_{jk}=(\delta_{ij}H_k+\delta_{ik}H_j-\delta_{jk}H_i)/H$. Every other type vanishes because $g$ is diagonal and time-independent. The derivatives use [F3] and the positivity of $H$.

Any other torsion-free, $g_H$-compatible connection $\widehat
abla$ differs from $
abla$ by the tensor $C(X,Y):=\widehat
abla_XY-
abla_XY$. Torsion-freeness gives $C(X,Y)=C(Y,X)$, while subtracting the two compatibility identities gives $C_{XYZ}:=g_H(C(X,Y),Z)=-C_{XZY}$. Thus $C_{XYZ}=C_{YXZ}=-C_{YZX}=-C_{ZYX}=C_{ZXY}=C_{XZY}=-C_{XYZ}$, so $C=0$ by nondegeneracy of $g_H$. Therefore the displayed connection is unique. Its trace is $\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha i}=\Gamma^0{}_{0i}+\sum_{k=1}^3\Gamma^k{}_{ki}=-H_i/H+3H_i/H=2H_i/H$, while $\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha0}=0$.

In the Ricci formula, $\partial_i\Gamma^i{}_{00}=-\Delta H/H^5+5q/H^6$ by differentiating $-H_iH^{-5}$. The trace-product term is $\Gamma^i{}_{00}\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha i}=-2q/H^6$. The final product contraction $\Gamma^\alpha{}_{0\beta}\Gamma^\beta{}_{0\alpha}$ has two nonzero orders for each spatial $i$, namely $\Gamma^0{}_{0i}\Gamma^i{}_{00}$ and $\Gamma^i{}_{00}\Gamma^0{}_{i0}$; each is $H_i^2/H^6$, so its subtraction contributes $-2q/H^6$. Thus $\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=q/H^6-\Delta H/H^5$.

For $\operatorname{Ric}_{0i}$, the derivative terms vanish because all coefficients are time-independent and $\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha0}=0$. In the trace-product term, a nonzero $\Gamma^\alpha{}_{0i}$ requires $\alpha=0$, but then $\Gamma^\beta{}_{\beta0}=0$. In the last contraction, the only potentially nonzero first factors are $\Gamma^0{}_{0j}$ or $\Gamma^j{}_{00}$; their paired factors have a lower time-space connection slot that vanishes. Hence $\operatorname{Ric}_{0i}=0$.

For spatial $i,j$, $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=(\delta_{ki}H_j+\delta_{kj}H_i-\delta_{ij}H_k)/H$. Differentiating and summing $k$ gives $\partial_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=2H_{ij}/H-2H_iH_j/H^2-\delta_{ij}\Delta H/H+\delta_{ij}q/H^2$. The trace term is $-\partial_j\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha i}=-2H_{ij}/H+2H_iH_j/H^2$, using the commuting mixed partials of [F4]. The other trace product is $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha k}=(4H_iH_j-2\delta_{ij}q)/H^2$.

In the last Ricci contraction, the time-index product is $\Gamma^0{}_{i0}\Gamma^0{}_{j0}=H_iH_j/H^2$. The spatial numerator is $(\delta_{ai}H_b+\delta_{ab}H_i-\delta_{ib}H_a)(\delta_{bj}H_a+\delta_{ba}H_j-\delta_{ja}H_b)$. Summing over $a,b$ gives the nine terms $H_iH_j,H_iH_j,-\delta_{ij}q,H_iH_j,3H_iH_j,-H_iH_j,-\delta_{ij}q,-H_iH_j,H_iH_j$, hence the spatial product is $(5H_iH_j-2\delta_{ij}q)/H^2$. Including the time product, the full product before the Ricci minus sign is $(6H_iH_j-2\delta_{ij}q)/H^2$. Combining this with step 3.3 gives $\operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=-\delta_{ij}\Delta H/H+(\delta_{ij}q-2H_iH_j)/H^2$.

Contracting the Ricci table with $g^{00}=-H^2$ and $g^{ij}=H^{-2}\delta_{ij}$ gives $g^{00}\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=-q/H^4+\Delta H/H^3$ and $\sum_{ij}g^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=q/H^4-3\Delta H/H^3$. Their sum is $S=-2\Delta H/H^3$.

A matter tensor $T_m^{ab}$ is a $C^1$ symmetric contravariant two-tensor field; a current $j^a$ is a $C^1$ vector field. The **formal sourced Maxwell equations** are $dF=0$ and $\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$. The **matter exchange equation** is $\nabla_aT_m^{ab}=F^b{}_cj^c$. The **formal Einstein equation** is

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa\bigl(T_{m,ab}+T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}\bigr).$$

Here $T_{m,ab}$ is obtained by lowering both indices with $g$. Each displayed equation is a pointwise mathematical condition on the supplied fields with the regularities stated above. A formal Einstein–Maxwell–matter solution is a tuple satisfying whichever of these equations are explicitly assumed on the stated open domain; no existence or uniqueness of such a tuple is asserted.

For $a>0$, integer $m$ and integer $n\ge1$, define the rational regime by

$$
a^{m/n}:=(a^{1/n})^m,
$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique positive root of $s^n=a$ in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and integer powers include reciprocals for negative $m$. This is [[def-rational-power]]; [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] proves independence of the fraction representative and [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives the rational exponent laws. The supplementary convention is $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$; $0^0$ and negative powers of zero remain undefined.

The separate real regime is [[def-real-power]]: for $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, with the laws of [[thm-real-power-laws]]. For $x>0$ set $0^x=0$; no arbitrary real power is assigned to a negative base. The real-power laws are supplied by that theorem, not inferred from the rational root formula. Use the real-number structure of [[def-real-numbers]].

In particular $s(q)=q^{1/2}$ for $q>0$ is the unique positive solution of $s(q)^2=q$. Its smoothness and derivative are a separate well-definedness result, not an assumption about fractional notation.

Use the energy-condition definitions of [[def-emg-pointwise-energy-conditions]] and the matter and Maxwell tensor definitions of [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. At every point of an oriented time-oriented Lorentzian domain, the Maxwell tensor $T_{\mathrm{EM}}$ of that definition is symmetric, trace-free, and satisfies WEC, NEC, SEC and DEC. Its observer energy density and energy flux in a positively oriented orthonormal rest frame are

$$u=\frac{|E|^2/c^2+|B|^2}{2\mu_0},\qquad \frac{E\times B}{\mu_0c},$$

and the DEC flux is future causal or zero. A charged-dust tensor with $\rho\ge0$ satisfies all four conditions. For a perfect-fluid tensor with rest energy density $\epsilon$ and pressure $p$, the exact pointwise conditions are

$$\mathrm{WEC}\iff \epsilon\ge0\text{ and }\epsilon+p\ge0,\quad \mathrm{NEC}\iff\epsilon+p\ge0,$$

$$\mathrm{SEC}\iff\epsilon+p\ge0\text{ and }\epsilon+3p\ge0,\quad \mathrm{DEC}\iff\epsilon\ge|p|.$$

At a point, finite sums of tensors satisfying any one of these conditions still satisfy that condition; in particular $T_{\mathrm{EM}}+T_m$ satisfies all four for nonnegative dust. No general matter positivity assumption is made, and adding $T_{\mathrm{EM}}$ to an arbitrary fluid need not repair a violated fluid inequality.

([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
